name: Israel and the fiery serpents
charge: Speaking against God and against Moses; loathing the bread from heaven
summary: Edom had refused them passage, and the soul of the people was much discouraged because of the way. They spoke against God and Moses: no bread, no water, and their soul loathed this light bread, which was angels’ bread. The Lord sent fiery serpents and many of the people of Israel died. The brass serpent on the pole was for the Israelites, to heal the Israelites, and Christ brought it to Nicodemus, one Israelite to another: the Son of man must be lifted up the way Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness.
offenseFull: They journeyed from mount Hor by the way of the Red sea to compass the land of Edom, and the soul of the people was much discouraged because of the way; since Edom refused passage and came out against them with a strong hand, Israel had to go around, and the way was longer than they wanted it to be (Numbers 21:4; Numbers 20:18-21). The people spoke against God and against Moses, asking why they had been brought up out of Egypt to die in the wilderness with no bread and no water, and saying that their soul loathed this light bread (Numbers 21:5). The bread they loathed was angels’ bread, rained on them from heaven every morning, prepared without their labour and able to agree with every taste (Psalms 78:25). No other nation on this earth takes its food as seriously as Israel; even the complaints over bread and water are a familiar mark of this people to this day, and you cannot put another nation in these scriptures. Paul sets it among the warnings: do not tempt Christ, as some of them tempted and were destroyed of serpents (1 Corinthians 10:9).
judgmentFull: The Lord sent fiery serpents among the people, and they bit the people, and many of the people of Israel died (Numbers 21:6). Fiery means poisonous, and the words of the verse should be read with the nation in view: the people bitten, the people dying, all of it is Israel. That detail settles an argument. A mixed multitude had come up with them, but the dying named here is Israel, because He gave His word to Jacob, His statutes and His judgments to Israel, and He has not dealt so with any nation (Psalms 147:19-20). The biting brought them back into the spirit at once: they confessed that they had sinned in speaking against the Lord and against Moses, and asked him to pray that the Lord would take away the serpents; and Moses prayed for the people (Numbers 21:7).

The serpents were not taken away. The Lord told Moses to make a fiery serpent and set it on a pole, and every man who was bitten would live when he looked on it; Moses made a serpent of brass, and any man bitten by a serpent lived when he looked on the serpent of brass (Numbers 21:8-9). That pole with a snake wrapped around it is the sign still painted on the side of an ambulance today, and it stands for healing because of this passage. The book of Wisdom says they were troubled for a small season to be admonished, having a sign of salvation to put them in remembrance of the commandment of the law; the man who turned toward it was not saved by the thing he saw, but by God, the Saviour of all (Wisdom of Solomon 16:5-7).

That brass serpent was for the Israelites, to heal the Israelites who were bitten for rebelling against God and against Moses, and Christ brought this passage to Nicodemus, a Pharisee and a ruler of the Jews, one Israelite to another: as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of man be lifted up, so that every man who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life (John 3:1, 14-15). The one who believes is defined where Peter defines it: every man who calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved, and the word is spoken to the men of Israel (Acts 2:21-22). As the bitten looked on the brass and lived, so Israel looks on the Son of man lifted up. The serpent itself became an idol centuries later, and Hezekiah broke it in pieces, which is entered under his name.

text.text: And they journeyed from mount Hor by the way of the Red sea, to compass the land of Edom: and the soul of the people was much discouraged because of the way.
And Edom said unto him, Thou shalt not pass by me, lest I come out against thee with the sword.

And the children of Israel said unto him, We will go by the high way: and if I and my cattle drink of thy water, then I will pay for it: I will only, without doing any thing else, go through on my feet.
And he said, Thou shalt not go through. And Edom came out against him with much people, and with a strong hand.
Thus Edom refused to give Israel passage through his border: wherefore Israel turned away from him.

And the people spake against God, and against Moses, Wherefore have ye brought us up out of Egypt to die in the wilderness? for there is no bread, neither is there any water; and our soul loatheth this light bread.
Man did eat angels’ food: he sent them meat to the full.
Neither let us tempt Christ, as some of them also tempted, and were destroyed of serpents.
And the Lord sent fiery serpents among the people, and they bit the people; and much people of Israel died.
He sheweth his word unto Jacob, his statutes and his judgments unto Israel.
He hath not dealt so with any nation: and as for his judgments, they have not known them. Praise ye the Lord.

Therefore the people came to Moses, and said, We have sinned, for we have spoken against the Lord, and against thee; pray unto the Lord, that he take away the serpents from us. And Moses prayed for the people.
And the Lord said unto Moses, Make thee a fiery serpent, and set it upon a pole: and it shall come to pass, that every one that is bitten, when he looketh upon it, shall live.
And Moses made a serpent of brass, and put it upon a pole, and it came to pass, that if a serpent had bitten any man, when he beheld the serpent of brass, he lived.
For when the horrible fierceness of beasts came upon these, and they perished with the stings of crooked serpents, thy wrath endured not for ever:
But they were troubled for a small season, that they might be admonished, having a sign of salvation, to put them in remembrance of the commandment of thy law.
For he that turned himself toward it was not saved by the thing that he saw, but by thee, that art the Saviour of all.
There was a man of the Pharisees, named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews:
And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up:
That whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have eternal life.
And it shall come to pass, that whosoever shall call on the name of the Lord shall be saved.
Ye men of Israel, hear these words; Jesus of Nazareth, a man approved of God among you by miracles and wonders and signs, which God did by him in the midst of you, as ye yourselves also know:
